sections.heading: What Ziffr is
sections.text: Ziffr is one place where a small team keeps its business numbers: revenue, new customers, open tickets, cash in the bank, customer satisfaction, hours worked. It collects each number from whoever knows it, keeps every value over time, and lets the team look at the numbers, talk about them and act on them.

sections.heading: The problem it solves
sections.text:
In most small companies the important numbers are scattered. Some sit in the accounting tool, some in the shop system, some in a spreadsheet on someone's laptop, and some only in a colleague's head. Every month someone sends emails asking for them, copies them into a slide, and hopes nobody typed a wrong digit. When a number looks odd, the discussion happens in a chat that nobody can find three months later.
Ziffr turns that into a routine that runs by itself:
Every number is described once. What it means, how it is counted, how often, what a good value is, and who is responsible for…

sections.heading: Who it is for
sections.text: Ziffr is built for teams of roughly five to a hundred people who want a clear view of how the business is doing without hiring a data team. Typical users are founders and managing directors, team leads who report their numbers each month, finance and controlling, and outside people such as a bookkeeper or a field worker who only send in one number now and then.

sections.heading: From a business intelligence tool
sections.text:
Business intelligence tools, such as Power BI, Tableau or Looker, are very good at drawing charts from data that already exists in a database. They assume someone has already collected, cleaned and modelled that data, and usually an analyst builds the reports.
Ziffr starts one step earlier. Many of the numbers a small team cares about are not in any database: they have to be asked for. Ziffr does the asking, checks the answers, and keeps a clean history. Its dashboards and decks are made by dragging and dropping, for people who are not analysts. Where a number does live in another system, a…

sections.heading: From a data warehouse
sections.text:
A data warehouse stores large amounts of raw records from many systems, every order and every click, so that specialists can analyse them. It needs engineers to build and maintain it.
Ziffr keeps only the numbers that matter for running the business, one value per period, with their targets, history and the decisions taken on them. It is not a place for millions of rows. If your company has a warehouse, Ziffr sits on top of it: a Feed reads the finished numbers from the warehouse and records them in Ziffr, where the rest of the team can see and discuss them.

sections.heading: From a spreadsheet
sections.text: A spreadsheet is flexible, but it does not ask anyone for a number, does not remind them, does not notice when a value looks wrong, and does not remember who changed what. Sharing one part of it with one person and another part with someone else is hard. Ziffr keeps every earlier value when one is replaced, records every change to who may see what, and shares each number on its own.

sections.heading: From a project or task tool
sections.text: Ziffr has questions and tasks, but only about numbers: each one is attached to a value or a time range of a Metric. It does not replace your project tool; it makes sure the conversation about a number stays next to that number.

sections.heading: What Ziffr is not
sections.text:
It is not an accounting system. It does not book transactions; it keeps the totals your accounting produces.
It is not a database for raw data. Each Metric has one value per period, optionally split into a Breakdown, such as revenue by country.
It does not run other people's programs. A Feed that reads your CRM runs on your side and only sends finished numbers to Ziffr.

sections.heading: The ideas behind Ziffr
sections.text: A handful of ideas explain almost everything Ziffr does. Once they are clear, the screens make sense on their own.

sections.heading: A number is described before it is collected
sections.text:
In Ziffr every number you track is a Metric. Before anyone can send in a value, the Metric is described: its name, what it means, its unit (euros, hours, percent), how often it is counted (each day, week, month, quarter or year), what a good value is, and who is responsible for it. That person is the Metric Owner.
This sounds like extra work, but it is what makes the numbers trustworthy. Everyone reads "Revenue" the same way, and nobody has to guess whether it includes tax.
A Metric can also be worked out from other Metrics, such as "Gross margin" from revenue and cost. That is a Derived…

sections.heading: Every value belongs to a period
sections.text:
One value of a Metric for one period is an Observation: "Revenue, October: 84,000 €". A value can carry a Breakdown that splits it, such as revenue by country, and a Metric can also have a Target Series (a budget per month) and Projections (values expected for coming periods).
When a second value arrives for the same period, the Metric's Submission Rule decides what happens: the new value replaces the old one, the two are added up, both are kept, or the second one is refused.
When a longer period is shown, the Aggregation decides how values combine: revenue is added up, a satisfaction score…

sections.heading: Someone gives each value
sections.text:
The people who send in values are Submitters. A Submitter can be a Member of the team, a Guest, a Contact who never logs in (a bookkeeper or a shop manager), or a Feed, a program that reads another system.
Values arrive through a Source: the personal form link, email, Slack, or the API. Ziffr knows who may send which number. Behind every value stands a Token, the standing permission that links one Submitter to one Metric. People never see tokens; they simply answer the message they got.

sections.heading: Ziffr asks, reminds and checks
sections.text:
A Workflow is the path a Metric's value takes each period. A typical one, such as "Monthly finance close", does this:
1. Ask. When the period ends, Ziffr sends each Submitter a Prompt: "What was revenue in October?"
2. Remind. Before the Due Date, counted in working days (for example the 3rd working day), Ziffr reminds whoever has not answered.
3. Escalate. If the value is still missing, an Escalation asks the person's Stand-in or tells the Metric Owner. People who are Away are skipped and their Stand-in is asked instead.
4. Check. A value that changes much more than usual, or falls outside…

sections.heading: Good and bad are defined, not guessed
sections.text:
Each Metric has a Target Range, the band its values should stay within, and a Polarity: whether higher is better (revenue), lower is better (cost), or closer to the target is better (stock level). From that, Ziffr colours values green or red, works out Attainment (how far a value reaches its target, as a percentage where higher is always better, by ratio or by distance to the target), and spots Unusual Values.
A Comparison sets the latest value against an earlier span: the previous period, or the same time last week, month, quarter or year, both as a difference and in percent.

sections.heading: Everyone sees what was shared with them, nothing more
sections.text:
Visibility is at the heart of Ziffr. Each person has a Workspace Role:
Owner: manages the Workspace, its settings, its people and billing.
Admin: the same as an Owner, except billing and removing Owners.
Member: creates and shares Metrics, dashboards and decks.
Guest: sees only what is shared with them, answers questions and sends in values, and creates nothing.
Metrics and dashboards are given to people or to Groups (such as "Management" or "Sales") with a Share. Someone with a Share is a Viewer, who can look, or an Editor, who can also change things. Sharing a dashboard also lets people see…

sections.heading: Nothing is lost
sections.text: When a value is replaced or corrected, the earlier one is kept as a Superseded Value. Everything people build (widgets, dashboards, decks, Metric descriptions) keeps its Versions, so you can go back. A dashboard's Snapshot keeps what it showed at the end of a week, month, quarter, half-year or year, so the numbers in last quarter's board meeting, or in the annual review, never change afterwards. The Audit Log records who changed who may see or do what, and which decisions were taken on numbers, and nobody can change it.

sections.heading: Questions stay with the number
sections.text: When a number raises a question, you assign an Action on that value: a Question ("Why is cost so high this month?") or a Task ("Renegotiate the shipping rate"). The Assignee answers in the action's Thread, by email or on Slack. If the value itself was wrong, the answer can propose a Correction, which takes effect once the Metric Owner accepts it.

sections.heading: How Ziffr is built
sections.text: You do not need to know how Ziffr works inside to use it. This chapter is for the people who decide whether to trust it with the company's numbers, and for anyone curious.

sections.heading: The big picture
sections.text:
Think of Ziffr as a house with one front desk. People and programs come in through different doors, but every one of them is sent to the same front desk, which checks who they are and what they may see or change. Behind the desk sits one archive where all numbers are kept.
The doors. The web app you use in the browser; email and Slack, where people answer Prompts; the API, through which programs and Feeds send values; and the MCP Server, which lets an AI assistant read numbers and send values.
The front desk. One set of rules decides, for every request, who is asking, in which Workspace, and…

sections.heading: Workspaces keep teams apart
sections.text: A Workspace is one team's own space: its people, Metrics, dashboards, decks, Themes and Connectors. A person can belong to several Workspaces, for example a bookkeeper who works for three companies, and switches between them. What happens in one Workspace never shows up in another.

sections.heading: What runs on its own
sections.text:
Some things happen without anyone clicking:
Every morning, in the Workspace's time zone, Ziffr works through the Workflows: who needs to be asked, reminded or escalated today.
Every few minutes, it sends waiting emails and tries again when one could not be sent.
When a period is complete, dashboards that are set up for it take their Snapshot.
Each message Ziffr sends is a Delivery, and every Delivery is listed in the Outbox, so you can always check what was sent to whom.

sections.heading: Programs only get what they need
sections.text:
Programs never use a person's password. They use an Access Key, made by a person for one purpose (for example, only sending values), valid for one Workspace and ending on a set date. A Feed uses a Feed Key, which can only record values for the Feed's own Metrics and cannot even read those values back. Every call a program makes is written into the Access Log.
When Ziffr sends something outside, such as a message on Slack or a dashboard behind a View Link, it sends only what is needed for that purpose.

sections.heading: Where Ziffr runs
sections.text:
Ziffr can be run for you or on your own servers. Either way, Ziffr itself only talks to its database and to the mail and Slack services you set up. A Feed that reads your CRM or your data warehouse runs on your side, with your credentials; Ziffr never holds the passwords to your other systems.
The people who run Ziffr on their own servers find the technical details in the guide "Running Ziffr yourself".

chapters.title: Connecting Ziffr to people and systems

sections.heading: Connecting Ziffr to people and systems
sections.text: Ziffr is only as good as the numbers that reach it. This chapter shows the ways numbers come in, the ways Ziffr reaches people, and the ways numbers go back out.

sections.heading: How numbers come in
sections.text:
Each Metric says which Sources it accepts. You can turn on several for the same Metric.
Every value goes through the same checks, whichever way it came: the Submission Rule, Approval of Unusual Values and Locks.

sections.heading: How Ziffr reads a number you send
sections.text:
Ziffr reads every number the same way, whichever way it came in: a reply, the form link, a pasted Breakdown or a Target Series.
Either way of writing works. 1,5 and 1.5 are both one and a half; 1.234,5, 1,234.5, 1 234,5 and 1'234.5 are all the same number. You may add a sign (-5, +5) or k and M (2,5k is 2,500).
One case depends on your Workspace. A single dot or comma followed by exactly three digits, such as 1.500, could be either. Ziffr reads it the way your Workspace writes numbers (its Number Style, see Workspace settings): fifteen hundred where you write 1.234,5, one and a half where you…

sections.heading: The personal form link
sections.text:
Every Submitter has a personal link for each Metric they send in. It needs no password, which is why Contacts such as an outside bookkeeper can use it. The link only lets them send values for their own Metrics: for the current period, or for an earlier one Ziffr asked them for.
If Ziffr cannot read what you typed, it says so under the field, with an example such as "Type a number, such as 88 or 1,250." What you typed stays in the field so you can correct it, and the cursor goes back to it.

sections.heading: Feeds: numbers from other systems
sections.text:
A Feed is a small program that reads a number from another system and sends it to Ziffr, for example the value of open deals from HubSpot every night. A Feed belongs to the Workspace, not to a person, so it keeps working when the colleague who set it up leaves. Its values appear under its own name, such as "HubSpot".
Only Owners and Admins create Feeds. Your technical colleague, or whoever looks after your systems, runs the Feed where you like: on a server, in a scheduled job or in an automation tool. Ziffr comes with two ready-made kinds: one for people who write a little code, and one that…

sections.heading: An AI assistant
sections.text: The MCP Server lets an AI assistant read the Metrics you may see, send in values and build dashboards. An assistant on the internet, such as Claude.ai, connects by your Ziffr's address and you approve it (Connecting an assistant); one on your own computer uses an Access Key you create. The assistant sees no more than you allow. What to ask it, and the ready-made requests it offers, are in Working with an assistant.

sections.heading: How Ziffr reaches people
sections.text:
A Connector links Ziffr to an outside service people already use. Through it, Ziffr sends Prompts, reminders, questions, tasks and replies, and brings the answers back.
Email sends real messages in the look of your team default Theme: its logo (a PNG or JPEG; otherwise the Workspace's name), accent colour and footer, readable in light and dark mode, with the same words as plain text beside it. Links are buttons or a few words, not long addresses. Replies record the number, answer in a Thread or propose a Correction. See Decks and Themes.
Slack is connected once per Workspace by an Owner or…

sections.heading: Send yourself a test message
sections.text:
To check how Ziffr reaches you, send yourself a Test Message by email, Slack or Telegram. It goes only to you: to the address you signed in with, or to the Slack and Telegram account you linked. The words are always the same (the Workspace's name and the way you tested), nothing in it can be answered, and Quiet Hours do not hold it. It shows in the Outbox marked Test.
You can send up to 3 test messages by one way in 10 minutes, and up to 20 a day in all (5 a day in a trial). Over a limit, Ziffr says which one and how long until you can try again.
When a way is not set up, the test stays in…

sections.heading: How numbers go out
sections.text:
Dashboards and decks are shared inside the team with Shares.
View Links show one dashboard or deck to someone outside the team, such as an investor or your advisory board, without a login. A View Link ends on a set date, can be revoked, and shows either live numbers or the numbers as they were when it was made.
Decks are exported as PowerPoint or PDF for meetings and email.
Programs can read Metrics and dashboards through the API with an Access Key, limited to what the key's person may see.

sections.heading: Templates: starting points
sections.text: You rarely have to start from an empty page in Ziffr. Several kinds of starting points help you describe Metrics, draw them and build dashboards. All of them are copied when you use them: changing the starting point later does not change what you already made.

sections.heading: The Metric Catalog
sections.text:
The Metric Catalog is a library of ready-made Metric descriptions, grouped by area: Finance, Sales, Customers, Marketing, Product, Operations, Support and People. Each one already says what the number means, its unit, how often it is counted, whether higher or lower is better, and a sensible target range.
Picking "Monthly recurring revenue" from the catalog copies its description into a new Metric of your own. From then on it is yours: change anything you like, there is no link back to the catalog. Ziffr also uses your Workspace Profile (your industry, who you sell to, your size) to suggest…

sections.heading: Widget Templates
sections.text:
A Widget Template is a starting point for one Widget: a way of drawing a number, with its settings, and an open place for the Metric. Ziffr ships these:
Anyone can save a Widget they made, with its words and annotations, as a team Widget Template. Only the person who saved it can change it; everyone else can use it.

sections.heading: Dashboard Templates
sections.text:
A Dashboard Template is a starting point for a whole dashboard: its Widgets, their layout and their words, with the Metrics left open. Ziffr ships eight:
Overview: four numbers at a glance, the first two also as trends against their targets.
One metric in depth: one Metric from every side: its latest value, where it sits against the target, its trend, its periods, its history and a forecast.
Two metrics side by side: two Metrics next to each other, and whether they move together.
Scorecard: six Metrics as gauges against their targets: what is on track and what is not, at a glance.
Trends…

sections.heading: Deck Templates and Workflow Templates
sections.text:
A Deck Template is a starting point for a whole deck: its slides with their Widgets, words and boxes, the Metrics left open as Slots. Save a deck as one with Save as Deck Template… in the deck editor, and start a deck from one on the Decks page (Decks and Themes). In the demo, where visitors may change it, you may save a deck as a Deck Template, save a slide as a layout and start a deck from a Deck Template, with plain words and no pictures; Workflow Templates stay off.
A Workflow Template is a starting point for a Workflow: its Due Date, steps and reminders, with the people left open. Its…

sections.heading: Slots and Placeholders
sections.text:
A template never contains your numbers. Instead it has:
Slots: the open places that you fill with a Metric when you use the template. One Slot can fill several Widgets, so choosing "Revenue" once puts it into every Widget that needs it.
Placeholders: words in a template's text that are filled in from the data, such as the Metric's name, the latest period or the change against last year. A headline like "Revenue rose 12% against last year" then stays correct for whatever Metric you choose.

sections.heading: Previews
sections.text: Before you place a template, Ziffr draws a small Preview. Because a template has no Metrics of its own, its Preview uses Sample Data: made-up numbers that are the same for everyone and never come from your Workspace. A saved Widget's or a Metric's Preview shows your own data.

sections.heading: Recipes
sections.text: A Recipe is a ready-made analysis that runs with one click on the Analysis Canvas, such as "What drives Cost?". It picks the right method and settings for you.

sections.heading: Themes
sections.text: A Theme is not a starting point, but it decides how everything with numbers looks: colours, fonts, how cards are drawn, and what every slide shows, such as your logo, a footer and slide numbers. The team has one default Theme; a dashboard or deck can use another. Owners and Admins change Themes.

sections.heading: Everything you work with
sections.text: This chapter lists the kinds of things you meet in Ziffr, what each one is for, and who may make one. Use it as a reference when a word in the app is new to you.

sections.heading: Getting started
sections.text: This chapter takes you from nothing to a team that sees its numbers each month. The Setup Guide, which opens by itself when you first join, walks you through the first steps; the routine then runs by itself.

sections.heading: Look around the demo first
sections.text: On the sign-in page, choose Try the demo under the form (the picture beside it shows the demo's Monthly overview dashboard; on a phone the form comes first and the picture is left out). It opens a made-up online shop with fifteen people, without an account. Its numbers move with today's date, so last month's cost spike is always last month. The monthly numbers go back three and a half years and the weekly ones three years, with a December peak and a few links worth finding (support tickets before refunds, a campaign that lifted new leads, marketing spend that stopped bringing new customers),…

sections.heading: When the demo lets you change things
sections.text:
Only a Ziffr that is a demo and nothing else can do this, and only where the person who runs it switched on Visitors may change the demo (off by default; see Installation settings). A demo that sits beside real Workspaces, such as the one on app.ziffr.net or on a company's own Ziffr, is always read-only, so that nobody ever writes into a database that holds real numbers.
It is shared. Everyone in the demo uses the same made-up company. What you change, every other visitor sees, and what they change, you see. So do not type anything private or anything you would not want a stranger to read,…

sections.heading: Trying values in a demo that can be changed
sections.text: A public demo may let visitors try the work around a value. Then the line above every page says what you change is shared with every visitor and gone when the demo starts fresh, with the time to the next fresh start, and nothing is sent. You can type a value on a Metric's page, use a form link, paste from a spreadsheet, fill in for someone, ask yourself for a value with Ask me now, answer a Prompt as the person it went to (in the Outbox or the Sources simulators), approve, send back, confirm or correct a value, propose a Correction and accept it, lock or reopen a period, close a Workflow's…

sections.heading: Trying Metrics, questions and sharing in a demo that can be changed
sections.text: In the same demo you can also define a Metric (from the catalog, from scratch, as a copy or calculated from other Metrics), change its description, Sources, targets and projections, put Tags on it, and archive it and bring it back. You can ask a Question or give a Task to one of the demo's people, reply as that person, close it or mark it done, share a Metric or dashboard of yours with a person or a Group, ask for access to something and grant it as its owner, make a Group of your own and choose who is in it, and set a person's way of being asked (an email, Slack or Telegram message goes to…

sections.heading: Start your Workspace
sections.text:
Sign in with your work email: Ziffr sends you a sign-in link (on hosted Ziffr the sign-in page also offers a trial of your own, next to the demo; on a Ziffr that somebody else runs it has no trial), and the page then says Check your email with the address it went to; Use another address takes you back to the form. Then give your Workspace a name, such as your name, your team or your company, and choose Create workspace. You become its Owner and can invite others later. If a colleague already uses Ziffr, ask them to invite you instead, so you join their Workspace.
A new Workspace opens on the…

sections.heading: The Setup Guide
sections.text: The Setup Guide is a short list of five steps that sets a Workspace up: About you, Starting point, Ways in and out, First Metric and Team. It lives at Set up your Workspace (the address /setup), shows the steps in a bar at the top with each one's state in words (Done, Skipped, To do, Comes next), and every step can be skipped. On a phone the bar is one line, "Step 2 of 5", over a strip with one segment per step; tap a segment to open that step. Go to Ziffr leaves it at any time, and the guide never blocks the app. The first time you open the guide on a phone, one short note comes before the…

sections.heading: About you
sections.text:
About you asks plain questions, one to a row, each optional and each saying what it is for. Choose Skip this question to leave one open, Skip to skip the whole step, or Save and go on.
The Workspace's time counts as answered once an Owner or Admin has saved it, even when it is UTC. A Member sees what the Owners and Admins said about the business, read-only, and answers only their own function.
What you answer stays in this Workspace. It is not sent to Ziffr's makers or to anyone else. It is used only inside this Workspace, to suggest Metrics, Packs and settings that fit and who is asked for…

sections.heading: Starting point
sections.text:
This step is for Owners and Admins, and asks how you want to begin. A Member never sees it. Nothing is installed or made until you press a button.
A Workspace that has Metrics already says "You have 4 Metrics. Start from a Pack anyway?" and still offers everything. A trial is no different: the step is To do until you choose, and a Pack stays within the trial's limits. The Start from a Pack card names your function from About you when you gave one ("Get ready-made Metrics for Finance."). On a phone the two buttons fill the width of their cards.

sections.heading: Ways in and out
sections.text:
Each of the last three steps opens with a sentence saying what it is, why you would do it and that you can skip it. On a phone their fields and buttons are 44 px tall with 16 px text (so Safari does not zoom in), the buttons fill the width with the main one on top and Skip under it, and cards, lists and links stack one to a line.
This step asks two questions on one screen. How should numbers come in? lists the ways a number reaches Ziffr, one card each, with its state in words:
Send me a test sends one Test Message to you, and the card says what came of it: sent, waiting to be sent, or kept…

sections.heading: First Metric: try the whole loop
sections.text:
First Metric shows that Ziffr and you can reach each other, in both directions, with one real Metric: the first one you made in the guide, one you pick with Another Metric (only Metrics you own that take values are listed), or, in a trial, the example.
When a trial's Owner reaches this step and the trial has no Metric yet, Ziffr makes the example, and the step says what it is: the Test Metric Cups of coffee, asked once a day, with a dashboard of its own. To use your own Metric instead, choose the link to make a Metric. Once a Metric has been deleted in the trial, Ziffr makes nothing by itself…

sections.heading: Team
sections.text:
This step is for Owners and Admins; a Member and a Guest never see it. It does the work of the Members and Groups page in one place, and everything it does is also there afterwards.
The step ticks once someone beside you is in the Workspace, an invitation is waiting, Domain Joining is on, or a Contact is asked for at least one Metric. A Contact that only exists does not count. Revoking the last invitation later does not reopen a finished guide.
In a trial, invitations open once the Owner has sent in a first value of their own. Until then the fields are greyed out, and a box right above them,…

sections.heading: The Setup line and opening by itself
sections.text:
A new Workspace opens on the Setup Guide, because there is nothing else to look at yet. Someone who joins a Workspace, by invitation or because their company's domain may join, is led to the guide once as well, and sees only the short version: About you and Ways in and out. After that the guide never opens by force again: Go to Ziffr is always one click away, and the guide never blocks the app.
While you have steps left, a thin line above every page (except the new Metric page opened from the guide, which says its own next step) says how far you are: "Setup: 2 of 5 done. Next: Ways in and…

sections.heading: Where would you like to start?
sections.text:
While there is nothing to look at yet, Ziffr's home asks Where would you like to start? instead of showing an empty dashboard. This is so when you have no dashboard (or only the untouched example of a trial, which you did not choose as your Home) and see no other Metric. You are offered only what your role allows:
As soon as you have a dashboard of your own, a Metric or a value in the example, or you chose a Home, Ziffr opens as usual. A Guest with nothing shared sees "Nothing has been shared with you yet". The demo never shows this screen.

sections.heading: In a trial, in the demo and on a Ziffr you run
sections.text:
On hosted Ziffr, a trial opens the same guide, with its own limits. Leaving it before you have a Metric leads to Where would you like to start?. See Starting a Workspace.
In the demo there is no guide, no line and no redirect; Set up your Workspace goes back to the dashboard, and the guided tour is the demo's own.
On a Ziffr you run yourself the guide is the same and depends on nothing hosted: Ziffr's own Packs come with it, and the ways read this Ziffr's own settings, so a Test Message goes through its own mail server, Slack app and Telegram bot. A way it lacks is said in words, with who…

sections.heading: What comes after the Setup Guide
sections.text: The guide gets one Metric asking and answering, and your first colleagues in. What follows is the routine, and none of it needs the guide.

sections.heading: Describe more Metrics
sections.text:
Go to Metrics and choose New metric (the Setup Guide's Starting point may have made the first ones already). The easiest start is the Metric Catalog: pick a number you already track, such as "Revenue" or "Customer satisfaction". Ziffr fills in its description, and you check:
Name and description: would a new colleague understand exactly what is counted?
Period: daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly or yearly. A number reported once a quarter, such as a survey score or board figures, is quarterly: Ziffr then asks for it once a quarter.
Target Range and Polarity: what a good value is, and whether…

sections.heading: Invite more people, and set the time later
sections.text:
The Team step does the first round. Later, under Workspace → Members and Groups, invite colleagues by email or with a link and choose their role:
Member for people who build dashboards and describe Metrics,
Guest for people who only look at what you share with them and send in their numbers,
Admin for someone who helps you manage the Workspace.
People who only send in a number, such as an outside bookkeeper, can be added as Contacts. They need no login and use their personal form link, email or Slack. Create Groups such as "Management" or "Sales" so you can share with many people at…

sections.heading: Let Ziffr ask for the numbers
sections.text:
Under Workspace → Workflows, create a Workflow such as "Monthly numbers": when to ask, when to remind, on which working day a value is due, who is asked when it is late, what counts as unusual, and who approves. Then assign it to your Metrics.
From now on, Ziffr sends the Prompts by itself. Each person chooses under Your Deliveries (their own menu at the bottom of the sidebar) whether they get them by email, on Slack or on Telegram, and enters the dates they are Away. The Ways in and out step above already saved your own choice there.

sections.heading: Build a dashboard
sections.text:
Go to Dashboards and choose Create dashboard. Start from a Dashboard Template, such as Overview, and fill its Slots with your Metrics, or start empty and drag Metrics from the Pool on the side. Each Metric can be drawn in different ways; pick the Widget Template that tells its story best.
Give the dashboard an introduction, then Share it with a Group. Everyone you share it with can see the Metrics on it. Choose your Home dashboard, the one Ziffr opens on.

sections.heading: Ask about a number
sections.text: When a value looks odd, open it and assign a Question to the person who knows: "Why did returns double in March?" They answer in the Thread, by email, on Slack or by Telegram, and the answer stays with the March value for anyone who looks later.

sections.heading: Close the month
sections.text: At the end of each period, check the Unusual Values waiting for Approval, then lock the period. If your dashboard should keep what it showed, take a Snapshot, or let the dashboard take one by itself once every Metric on it is locked. Need slides for the board? Make a Deck from your Widgets and export it as PowerPoint or PDF.

sections.heading: Put Ziffr on your phone or desktop
sections.text:
Ziffr installs as an app from the browser: it then opens from your home screen or dock in a window of its own, without the browser's address bar. There is nothing to download from an app store.
iPhone and iPad (Safari): open Ziffr, choose the Share button, then Add to Home Screen.
Android (Chrome): open Ziffr, choose the menu (⋮), then Add to Home screen or Install app.
Computer (Chrome or Edge): open Ziffr and choose the install icon at the right of the address bar, or Install Ziffr in the browser's menu. On a Mac, Safari offers File → Add to Dock.
The installed app is the same Ziffr as in…

sections.heading: Screens made for a larger screen
sections.text:
A phone is good for looking at numbers and for quick answers; building is easier with a larger screen. On a phone these screens show a note at the top that says "This is easier on a larger screen." and why: editing a dashboard, the deck editor, Workflows, the tabs of Connectors except the Outbox, Packs, the Playground, Installation settings, Analyze, New metric and the import of a Workspace Export. Nothing is switched off: the screen is below the note and you may use it.
The note offers up to two things:
Send me the link emails the address of this screen to you, and to nobody else, so you can…

sections.heading: What to do next
sections.text:
Bring in numbers from other systems. Ask whoever looks after your systems to set up a Feed for numbers that already live in your CRM, shop or data warehouse. See Connecting Ziffr.
Connect Slack. If your team works in Slack, an Owner or Admin connects it under Workspace → Connectors.
Show the numbers outside. Send investors or advisors a View Link to a dashboard.
Set up your look. Owners and Admins add your logo, colours and fonts as a Theme.

sections.heading: The Metrics screens
sections.text:
Every number your team tracks is a Metric. This chapter walks through every screen about Metrics: the list, describing a new one, a Metric's own page with its tabs, and the small form a Submitter opens to send in a value. Open them with Metrics in the sidebar.
Not everyone sees the same Metrics. You see a Metric when you own it, when it is shared with you or with one of your Groups, when it is on a dashboard or deck shared with you, or when you send in its values. Being an Owner or Admin of the Workspace does not show you every Metric by itself.

sections.heading: How colours and arrows work
sections.text:
The same rule holds on every Metric screen, and on dashboards too:
Green and red only say whether a value is on target. A small label next to a value reads "On target" (green) or, when it is off target (red), what is wrong: "Too high" for a Metric where lower is better, "Too low" where higher is better, and "Above target" or "Below target" for a target range with no better side. When a Metric has no target, there is no label. A Widget that shows a Metric by quarter or year judges each quarter against that quarter's target; point at the label to see which target applies (see Show by in the…

sections.heading: The Metrics list
sections.text:
The list shows every Metric you may see, one row each.
Under a Metric's name, its Tags show as small chips, at most three and then "+2". Above the list, the Tag row offers the Tags of the Metrics you may see, each with how many Metrics of this view carry it (Archived Metrics count under Archived only). Click a Tag to show only the Metrics that carry it; click a second one to narrow further, so "finance" and "monthly" show the Metrics that carry both. Clear shows all again. The picked Tags are in the page address, so a filtered list can be bookmarked or sent to someone, who sees only the…

sections.heading: Download values
sections.text: Each row has a checkbox (on a phone, in the card's top right corner). Tick the Metrics you want and a bar appears at the foot of the screen with how many are selected, Delete… (not for a Guest; see Deleting a Metric), Download values and Clear. Download values gives you one CSV file with every value of those Metrics, one row per value, oldest first for each Metric. The box at the head of the table (on a phone, Select all in the bar) ticks every Metric the list shows, after the Tag and Archived filters; under Archived you can download Archived Metrics, whose values are kept. One file holds at…

sections.heading: Paste values from a spreadsheet
sections.text:
Paste values in the Metrics list, or Paste history on a Metric's History tab, opens a page for values you already keep in a spreadsheet. Copy the cells in Excel, Google Sheets, LibreOffice or Numbers and press Ctrl+V (⌘V on a Mac) anywhere on the page, or paste them into the text box. Ziffr reads only the cells' text: no add-on and no connection to Microsoft or Google is needed.
Nothing is recorded until you confirm. Ziffr first shows what each value would do.

sections.heading: From a file
sections.text: Instead of pasting, drop a file on the box or choose Or choose a file: a CSV file (.csv, .tsv or .txt), an Excel workbook (.xlsx, .xls) or an OpenDocument one (.ods). The file is read in your browser, and only its cells are sent, exactly as if you had pasted them, so the preview and the limits are the same. A workbook's first sheet is read, cells as they are shown (a cell formatted as 2.5 % reads as 2.5 %); with several sheets, pick another under sheet. A CSV file may hold at most 256 KB and a workbook at most 10 MB.

sections.heading: A template to fill in
sections.text:
Under the box, Download a template saves a CSV file that already names your Metrics, so you only type the numbers. Pick one of three:
One value per row: the columns metric, period and value, one row for each Metric you may paste for, with its own current period filled in.
Metrics down, periods across: your Metrics of one period length (the most common one, or pick another next to it) and the last 12 periods as columns, oldest first.
One Metric's periods without a value: two columns, period and value, listing the periods in the last two years that have no value yet. Choose the Metric next to…

sections.heading: The layouts
sections.text:
Ziffr recognises three layouts and says above the preview which one it read, such as "Metrics as rows, periods as columns: 2 Metrics × 3 periods". When a paste fits two layouts, a link offers the other reading.
Metrics as rows, periods as columns, or the other way round. The first cell may be empty:
One value per row, with its Metric, period and value in any order of columns. A header row such as "Metric, Period, Value" is skipped. A column between them that is empty everywhere is fine:
Two columns, period and value, for one Metric. Paste history opens the page with its Metric chosen; on the…

sections.heading: How periods and numbers are read
sections.text:
Periods are read the way Ziffr reads an answer to a Prompt: "2026-10", "Oct-26", "October 2026", "Q3 2026", "KW 46", "2026-W46", or a date such as "2026-10-15", "15.10.2026" or "10/15/2026" in the order your Workspace writes dates. A date inside a period counts as that period, so "2026-10-15" is October for a monthly Metric. A period of another length than the Metric's (a month for a weekly Metric) is refused, and so is a period that has not begun yet. A spreadsheet's date number such as "46296" is never guessed.
Numbers are read in the Workspace's Number Style, as everywhere else. A currency…

sections.heading: The preview
sections.text:
The preview lists every value, grouped by Metric: its cell (such as C7), the period, the value as Ziffr will store it, the outcome, and why. Above it, a summary says how many values would be recorded and how many would not, such as "118 to record (4 of them unusual), 2 locked, 6 refused". The summary is also read out to screen readers.
In the demo, the personal form link of a Metric the demo came with opens only in a demo visit; a Metric you made there has none to open for anyone else.
You record values only for Metrics you submit for, through the same rules as the personal form link: the…

sections.heading: Record as history
sections.text: The Metric Owner, and an Owner or Admin who submits for the Metric, see Record as history for that Metric: "No Unusual Value check, marked as imported". It applies only to past periods that have no value yet. Those values become an Import: they skip the Unusual Value check and its Approvals and are marked as imported in the Metric's history. A period that already has a value, the current period, and a Locked period are handled as usual. Nobody else gets the choice, and asking for it any other way changes nothing.

sections.heading: Recording
sections.text: Record … values records them one after the other, per Metric in period order, so each month is checked against the one before as the paste left it. If something changed since the preview (a colleague recorded a value, a period was Locked), a value gets the outcome it gets now, marked "changed since the preview". The result lists what became of each value, with a link to each Metric. Paste more starts again.

sections.heading: Limits
sections.text:
A paste holds at most 256 KB of text and 2,000 values, and you may paste at most 10,000 values in 24 hours, across all your Workspaces. In the demo, where every visitor acts as the same made-up people, the day's limit is 500. A paste over a limit is refused whole, never cut. The result says how many values you may still paste today.
The list shows the Metrics in use. Once a Metric you may see is archived, two filters appear above the list: In use and Archived with their number. Archived lists only the Archived Metrics (see below).

sections.heading: New metric
sections.text:
On a phone the page says at the top that it is easier on a larger screen; see Screens made for a larger screen.
New metric opens a page with two ways to begin. You can change everything afterwards.
Start from scratch: an empty form, for a number nobody has described before.
Metric Catalog: a library of ready-made descriptions. Picking one copies its description into a new Metric of your own. It is yours from then on and does not follow later changes to the catalog. Besides the entries every Workspace has, it holds those of the Packs your Workspace installed, under each entry's category or the…

sections.heading: Finding a Metric in the catalog
sections.text: Each card shows the Metric's name, what it counts, its period, which way is good and its target. Click a card to open the form, already filled in. If nothing matches, try another word or start from scratch.

sections.heading: Your first metric, from the Setup Guide
sections.text:
When an Owner or Admin arrives from the Setup Guide, by Explore on my own or Make a Metric, the page says OK, from scratch. Let's do your first metric together and explains that a metric is one number you keep track of over time. The thin Setup line is left off here and on the form that follows, and so is the note that the screen is easier on a larger one (the form keeps it).
One line at the top of the form says what to do: check the name, or give one, and press Create metric at the bottom. The Metric becomes the guide's first Metric, and you are back in the guide. Back to the suggestions…

sections.heading: The form
sections.text:
The form is short: three parts, and More options below them for what you rarely change. The panel on the right says that you become the Owner: "The owner keeps the description up to date and accepts corrections to its values." Create metric saves it; Cancel goes back to the list.
What is it?
How do values arrive?
Target
More options
A folded section below Target. Opening it shows the fields below; leave it closed and Ziffr uses the defaults named in the table, which is what the form always used. While it is closed, its heading names every value that is not the default, such as "2 decimals ·…

sections.heading: A Metric's page
sections.text:
The top of the page shows the Metric's name, a Derived badge if it is calculated from other Metrics (Total if it adds up a list of them), and its description. Under it, How it is calculated opens the Metric's Calculation Note and, for a Derived Metric, its formula written with the names of the Metrics it uses; it is not shown when there is neither. If the formula uses a Metric that is not shared with you, the page says so instead of writing the formula. Below that are three boxes:
Latest: the most recent value with its period and on-target label.
Change vs. previous period: an arrow and a…

sections.heading: Handing a Metric over
sections.text:
Next to Owner in a Metric's Description, the Metric's owner, Owners and Admins see Hand over…. Pick the Member who takes it over, then Hand over. The Metric's owner can pick only people who already see the Metric (share it first otherwise); Owners and Admins can hand any Metric to any Member. Guests, Contacts and Access Keys never take a Metric over or hand one over: a program cannot change who owns a Metric.
Handing over a Total closes it: its new owner decides anew whether to open it. The new owner is told through their way of being reached, and not during their Quiet Hours. The previous…

sections.heading: The buttons at the top
sections.text:
A Metric's page has one main button, and the rest sit in the ⋯ menu.
On a phone, ⋯ stays beside the Metric's name when it is the only button. The Fill past periods dialogs fit the screen: the title and Close stay where they are, the rest scrolls inside the dialog, and each button sits under its text.

sections.heading: The chart
sections.text:
The chart draws the Metric's values over time. A daily Metric shows its last 90 days. The shaded band is the Target Range, a dashed line is Ziffr's forecast, and a ringed point marks a period that has a question or task.
Click a point to ask someone about it. A small box opens, "New Action about" that period, with the value:
See Actions for what happens next; the Questions and Tasks you asked also show on your Schedule under Asked by me, where finished ones are grey with a tick, never red. On a Metric's page and its period page, an Approval in the list of Actions reads as a plain question…

sections.heading: Comparisons
sections.text:
The Comparisons box sets the latest value against earlier spans.
At the top it shows the Value of the latest period, its Target ("(series)" when it comes from the Target Series) and its Attainment: how far the value reaches its target, as a percentage where higher is always better. Attainment is green from 100 % up, red below. It is computed one of two ways, set for the Workspace on Workspace → General and changed for one Metric under Edit details…. Point at the Attainment to see which:
By ratio divides the value by the target, or the target by the value when lower is better. With a target of…

sections.heading: Breakdown
sections.text:
A Breakdown splits one value into labelled rows, such as revenue by country. The box shows the rows of the latest period that has one, largest first. Buttons above it switch between the last six periods with a Breakdown.
When the rows add up to the total, a Share column shows each row's part. When they do not, a note says so: the total stays the Metric's value. Rates, for example, never add up. With no Breakdown yet, the box explains how to send one: add rows on the form, or send one line per row, such as "Germany 61,200".
A row can be a part of another row of the same Breakdown, such as a…

sections.heading: The Analysis tab
sections.text:
The tab is what Ziffr already knows about this one Metric, in three parts from top to bottom.
Ready for the Metric has a card for each analysis of the Metric alone that its history allows, worked out when you open the tab, each with its Takeaway. A card appears only when its analysis can answer: with too few values, or nothing to reach, there is no card and nothing is said about it. At most four analyses run for the page.
Where is the Metric heading? comes first and is the largest card: the history with the forecast dashed after it and its likely range as a band, the Takeaway (the sentence,…

sections.heading: The Targets tab
sections.text:
The Target Range applies to every period. On this tab you give single periods a target of their own, such as a monthly budget: the Metric's Target Series. You also enter Projections, values expected for future periods. Projections are always shown as projections and never count as real values.
The Metric Owner and the Metric's Editors change this tab. Everyone else sees a plain table of periods, targets and projections. A Derived Metric has no Target Series of its own. A formula can read the targets set here: see Reading a target.

sections.heading: The History tab
sections.text:
Latest values lists the last 12 values, oldest on top:
A Derived Metric has no values of its own, so it has no such list. If you submit values for the Metric on the web form, Paste history beside the heading opens Paste values for this Metric.
Questions and tasks lists every Action on this Metric that you may read, with its status (Open, Answered, Done for a finished task, or Closed), its period and its Assignee. Click one to open its Thread. With none yet, the tab reminds you to click a point on the chart.

sections.heading: A period's page
The Description tab
sections.text: The Description tab has four boxes: the Metric Description, the Retention, the Workflow, and who submits. A Derived Metric shows only its description.

sections.heading: Description
sections.text:
The box lists the Metric Description: owner, Tags, How it is calculated (the formula of a Derived Metric, written with the names of the Metrics it uses, and the Calculation Note; if the formula reads a Metric that is not shared with you, a line says so instead of naming it; "Not written down yet." when there is neither), period, format and decimals, which way is good and target. For other than Derived Metrics it also shows how values arrive and what happens to a second value.
Values arrive by can be changed right here by the owner and Editors: tick or untick Web form, Mail, Slack, Telegram…

sections.heading: Calculated from other Metrics
sections.text:
A Derived Metric is a number worked out from other Metrics, such as a margin, or the kilometres driven per day from a weekly odometer reading. Nobody is asked for it: it has a value in each period in which the Metrics it is made of have one.
To make one, choose New metric, then Calculated from other Metrics:
1. Give it a Name, and if you like a Description.
2. Build the Formula: click a Metric in the list to put it into the formula (it is written as its slug in curly brackets, such as {revenue}), and type + - /, brackets and numbers between them. The buttons change( ), prev( ) and target( )…

sections.heading: Adding up Metrics (a Total)
sections.text:
A Total is a sum over a list of Metrics it keeps, such as the Commit of every salesperson. Unlike a formula it does not name its Metrics in writing: you add and end them on its page, and past totals stay as they were.
To make one, choose New metric, then Calculated from other Metrics, then Add up Metrics:
1. Give it a Name.
2. Tick the Metrics under Which Metrics does it add up? You can add up 1 to 50 Metrics that you own or edit, that take values and that share a period, unit, number format and Aggregation. A Metric with Aggregation Does not combine (a rate) cannot be added up. Once you tick…

sections.heading: Retention
sections.text:
A Retention says how long the Metric keeps its values, and what then happens to older ones. The box shows what is in force ("none: values are kept for ever" until someone sets one). Nothing is ever condensed or deleted unless a person turns it on here.
The Metric Owner, Owners and Admins see the form. Choose Keep values for 2, 3, 5, 7 or 10 years (or Other, in months, at least 13 so that a comparison with last year always has its whole span), and Then:
Nothing: keep every value, which turns a Retention off.
Condense into longer periods: values older than the keep time become one Condensed…

sections.heading: Workflow
sections.text:
A Workflow is the path the Metric's value takes each period: who is asked, when they are reminded, who steps in, which values need Approval, and when the period locks. This box is described in detail in Workflows and approvals. In short:
The Workflow menu chooses one of the Workspace's Workflows, or None: values publish as they come. Only the Metric Owner changes it.
With a Workflow, the box shows the last period that has ended, its Due Date, and where its value is, such as "asked, waiting for the value" or "published and locked", with a link to open the Workflow.
Lock or Unlock the last…

sections.heading: Who submits
sections.text:
The Submitters of this Metric: who may send values for it. Ziffr recognises them by their Slack name or mail address, or by their personal form link. Each row shows the person and either Open form link (when the Web form is one of the Sources) or the link's code. A Stand-in who has been asked to step in is listed too, with a form link of their own.
Under each person a line says where their next Prompt will go and why, for example "Next request: by Slack", or "Can't reach: link Slack" when none of the ways this Metric accepts reaches them. The owner and Editors see it for everyone; anyone else…

sections.heading: Sharing a Metric
sections.text:
Share belongs to the Metric Owner. For each person, and for each Group ("including whoever joins later"), choose No access, Viewer or Editor.
Invite someone… at the bottom of the Share window is for someone who is not in the Workspace yet, such as when you are the only one in it. Owners and Admins enter an email address and choose Member or Guest (a Guest sees only what is shared with them), and Ziffr invites them the same way as the Members and Groups page: it emails the link when mail is set up and shows it to send yourself. A person is shared with once they have joined and appear in the…

sections.heading: Versions
sections.text:
⋯ → Versions opens a panel on the right that lists the Metric's description as it was after each change, newest first: who changed it, when, and what changed, such as "Changed its description", "Changed how it is calculated" or "Takes values from the Feed …". A change of how the Metric is calculated is always a Version of its own, so you can see when the number began to mean something else and what it said before. Changes by one person within ten minutes form one Version.
The Metric Owner can:
Restore an earlier Version. Restoring adds a new Version, so nothing is lost.
Name a Version, or…

sections.heading: Duplicating a Metric
sections.text:
Duplicate opens the new metric form, filled in from this Metric, titled "Duplicate …". The name gets "(copy)" added. The duplicate is a new Metric of yours with the same description, Sources and people who submit, and, if the original has one, a ticked Workflow box to keep the same Workflow. Values, Shares, Target Series and history stay with the original. Feeds are not copied: choose them again on the new Metric. Confirm with Create duplicate.
Duplicating is also the way to count a number in a different period, since a Metric's period is fixed once it has values.

sections.heading: Archiving a Metric
Deleting a Metric
sections.text:
Only the Metric Owner deletes a Metric. Deleting is for good: its values and their history, Breakdowns, targets, Projections, questions, tasks and form links go with it. If you only want the requests to stop, archive it instead; Archive instead is in the same window.
Open the Metric and choose ⋯ → Delete…. To delete several at once, tick them in the Metrics list and choose Delete… in the bar beside Download values (at most 50 at once).
1. Look at what can be deleted. The window lists the Metrics that can go and those that stay, each with the reason:
you are not its Metric Owner;
another…

sections.heading: Filling in a value for someone
sections.text:
When a Submitter has not sent a value, the Metric Owner or the owner of the Metric's Workflow can enter it for them. The value is recorded as the Submitter's, counts for them in their Schedule, the period's progress and the reports, and always shows who typed it: "Entered by Ben for Sara".
Fill in for … appears under the value on the period's page and in the Workflow box of the Metric's page, for the period the box shows, and on the Workflows page, under each Metric in Metrics on it, for the period the Workflow is working on. It is there only for someone who may fill in, and only for a…

sections.heading: Locks and corrections on a Metric
sections.text:
A Locked period takes no more values. When someone sends a value for it anyway, it is not recorded. Instead the Metric Owner gets a question, "… is locked. … sent … late: accept it as a correction?", with Accept and Decline. The sender sees that their value went to the Metric Owner as a proposed Correction.
Anyone answering a question or task about a value can also propose a Correction in its Thread. It takes effect only when the Metric Owner accepts it. The earlier value is then kept and shown struck through, and the corrected value goes through the Metric's Workflow again, so a locked…

sections.heading: The personal form link
sections.text:
Every Submitter who is a person or a Contact has a personal form link for each Metric they submit. It arrives with the first request and with every Prompt, and it opens without signing in: the link itself says who is sending. Keep it to yourself: anyone with it can submit.
The page is drawn in the look of the Workspace's team default Theme: a header row inside the form's card with its logo and the Workspace's name above an accent line, its colours and fonts, and its footer line at the bottom. If the Theme's accent is too pale to read on its cards, Ziffr uses a darker shade of it. Only that…

sections.heading: While a request waits
sections.text:
A form link records the current period or one you were asked for. A Workflow usually asks for the period that has just ended. As long as you have not answered, your form link records that period, as a reply to the request does.
For lists every period you were asked for that still waits, newest first, and the running period, marked such as this week. It starts at the newest period asked for. Pick another one before you press Submit. If only the running period was asked for, there is no list, and For says "(asked for)".
A period waits while Ziffr asked you (this link) for it, you have not…

sections.heading: On a phone
sections.text:
On a phone (under 640 px wide) the same link opens a shorter screen: the Metric's name, the period, one large number field and Submit. Add a breakdown (optional) shows the Breakdown field. After a value is recorded, one message says what happened and the field gives way to Send another value.
If you are also signed in, and the link is your own, the screen adds what the link alone does not show:
Last value, with its period: the newest value before the period picked under For, if one of the periods Record a value lists has one.
After saving, Next: … with the Metric and the period of your next…

sections.heading: Workflows and approvals
sections.text:
A Workflow is the path a Metric's value takes each period: who is asked, when they are reminded, who steps in, which values need Approval, and when the period locks. Several Metrics can share one, such as "Monthly finance close". This chapter covers the Workflows page, the Workflow box on a Metric's page, and the controls for approving, sending back, correcting and locking values.
Open the Workflows page from the sidebar: Workspace → Workflows. Owners, Admins and Members can look at every Workflow and create them. A Guest creates nothing and sees only the Workflows of the Metrics shared with…

sections.heading: The Workflows page
sections.text:
The page has three parts: the list of Workflows on the left, the steps of the chosen Workflow in the middle, with what happened in each period under them, and on the right the Metrics that use it and when it runs.
On a phone the page shows one thing at a time: first the list of Workflows, and when you choose one, its steps on a screen of their own, with All workflows at the top to go back. A note at the top says the page is easier on a larger screen; Look at it goes to the steps (see Screens made for a larger screen).

sections.heading: What happened, period by period
sections.text:
Under the steps, What happened, period by period shows a timeline for each period of the Workflow, the newest first and open, the earlier ones folded (the last four). Each period says how many values are in, such as "5 of 6 in" (the values and the Workflow's checklist Tasks to tick off count together), and whether it is published or locked. Under it are the events in order, with their day and time in the Workspace's time zone:
who was asked and reminded, grouped when close together: "Asked 6 people by Email, Slack and Telegram",
values that came in, with how many were in by then: "5 values…

sections.heading: Tell the owner when a period locks
sections.text: Ticking Tell the owner when a period locks (only the owner changes it, and it is off by default) sends the Workflow's owner a short summary by their Delivery Preference once every value the Workflow asks for in the period is locked: how many were in, and the Approvals and Questions about them, as far as the owner may see them. When the Workflow has checklist tasks, the summary also says how many are done: "3 of 4 checklist items done." Save the Workflow to keep the setting.

sections.heading: The list
sections.text:
Each Workflow shows its name, who owns it and how many Metrics use it (counting the Metrics you may see). Click one to open it.
New workflow creates one straight away, named "New workflow", with a sensible start that you then adjust:
due on the 3rd working day after the period,
remind 2 days before the Due Date,
on the Due Date, if the value is still missing, ask the Stand-in,
unusual if the value changes more than 30 % or falls outside the target,
an Approval step with nobody chosen yet,
publish and lock the period.
New from a template starts a Workflow from one of the team's Workflow…

sections.heading: The steps
sections.text:
The steps are drawn as a timeline, from top to bottom. Each step shows in words what it does, with its settings underneath. The owner moves a step with the arrows Earlier and Later, and takes it out with Remove step.
Ask always comes first and cannot be changed: "When the period ends, ask each submitter through their connector. While someone is away, their stand-in is asked." Ziffr sends each Submitter a Prompt, by email, on Slack or wherever that person gets their messages (see Your settings). A Feed is a program and is never asked.
Add step offers the other kinds:
Publish always comes last…

sections.heading: What happens to a value
sections.text:
Once a value is in, the Workflow does this:
1. Check. If the Workflow has a Check step, the value is compared with the period before and with its target. Values a Feed records for past periods that had none yet (an Import) are not checked.
2. Approval. If the value is unusual, or the Approve step says Every value, and the step names someone other than the Submitter, the first Approver gets an Approval task. Until it is approved, the value shows, marked as not approved yet.
3. Publish. A value that needs no Approval, or that every Approver has approved, is published, and locked if the Publish…

sections.heading: Metrics on it
sections.text:
The right side lists every Metric that uses this Workflow and that you may see. For each it shows:
the period being worked on (the last one that has ended) and its Due Date,
where the value is: Not started, Asked, waiting, In, not approved yet, Waiting for approval, Published, or Published and locked,
a note when there is one, such as why a value is unusual, who sent it back, or who unlocked the period and why,
who submits it (a Feed by its name) and, where chosen, their Stand-in.
Add Metrics… under the list picks Metrics for this Workflow right here. It offers the Metrics you own (not…

sections.heading: Asking Schedule
sections.text:
By default a Workflow runs with the Workspace's daily run, at the Workspace's hour. Under the Name and Due Date, Runs lets you give the Workflow its own time and days instead: choose On its own schedule.
The Ask step then says it in words, with the next run: "Runs every third day from 1 December 2026 at 14:00 (Europe/Berlin). Next: 4 December 2026." The schedule decides only when Ziffr runs the Workflow: Due Dates never move. A reminder or an Escalation whose day is not a run day goes out on the next run day, once. A run asks for the last period that ended, so a Workflow that runs less often…

sections.heading: When Workflows run
sections.text:
In a real Workspace, Workflows run by themselves once a day. The panel says when, such as "Workflows without their own schedule run every day at 07:00 (Europe/Berlin)". Owners and Admins set the time zone and the hour under Workspace → General, in Workspace time (see Workspace settings). Each run sends the day's Prompts, Remind steps and Escalations. A Workflow can also have an Asking Schedule of its own.
Running today's steps by hand answers with "Done: N requests, N reminders and N escalations made", and the Outbox shows which have gone out. The panel also shows the last run: when it was,…

sections.heading: Close the period
sections.text:
Close the period locks the last ended period for every Metric on this Workflow that has a value for it, all at once. Metrics still missing their value are left open, and so are values still waiting for Approval or sent back: closing a period approves nothing. Ziffr asks you to confirm first: late values and corrections then need Approval, and only a Metric's owner can unlock it. A message says how many Metrics were locked.
Only the Workflow's owner sees this button, and only while Metrics use the Workflow.

sections.heading: Filling in from the Workflows page
sections.text: Under each Metric in Metrics on it the Workflows page shows Fill in for … for the period the Workflow is working on, when a Submitter has not sent the value and you may fill in for them: you are the Metric Owner or the Workflow's owner, you see the Metric, and the period has no value yet. It is greyed out, with the reason, before the Due Date unless the Submitter is Away. It opens the same form as on the Metric's page and goes through the same checks: the core decides again when you save. A Guest is never shown it, and you see only the Metrics and Submitters you may see anyway. See Filling in…

sections.heading: A Metric's Workflow box
sections.text:
Each Metric's page has a Workflow box on its Description tab (see The Metrics screens). A Derived Metric has none: it is calculated, never sent in.
Choosing a different Stand-in takes effect at once: the person who stood in before can no longer send values for that Submitter. People enter their own Away dates under Your Deliveries (see Your settings); while someone is Away, their Prompts go to their Stand-in.
A Stand-in's answer to a request sent in someone's place is that person's value, entered by the Stand-in, and counts for the Stand-in only for the periods they were asked about.
Feeds…

sections.heading: Approving a value
sections.text:
When a value needs Approval, the Approver gets an Approval task. It appears on their Schedule (Schedule in the sidebar) and is sent to them like any task, by email or on Slack: "Approve Revenue for October 2026: 84,000 €, up 42.0 % on September 2026. Reply "approve", or "send back:" with what to check." In Ziffr itself the task shows only the question, the value with the period before and who submitted it, and the buttons Approve, Send back and Correct the value (see Actions); the reply words belong to the message.
On the task's page, the Approver sees a box, You approve this value:
The same…

sections.heading: Checking your own value
sections.text:
When a value needs Approval but nobody but you could give it, and the Approve step says let the submitter check it, you get a task instead (for a value someone entered for you, you are asked too: you did not type it, so checking it is a real check): "Check your value: 60 cups for 19 November 2026, up 900.0 % on 18 November 2026. Is that right?" On its page, a box Check your value has:
You can also reply "confirm", or "Correction: 6", to the task's message by email, Slack or Telegram. The task has no Mark done, Close Action or Reopen: only Confirm and Correct decide it. While the check waits,…

sections.heading: Locks
sections.text:
A Locked period takes no more values. A period is locked in one of three ways:
by the Publish step, when lock the period once published is ticked,
by the Metric Owner, with Lock … in the Metric's Workflow box,
by the Workflow's owner, with Close the period.
When a value arrives for a locked period, it is not recorded. It becomes a proposed Correction: the Metric Owner gets a question ("… is locked. … sent … late: accept it as a correction?") with Accept and Decline. The same holds for a Correction proposed in any Thread. An accepted Correction replaces the value, keeps the earlier one as a…

sections.heading: Finished period
sections.text: A Workflow's period is a finished period once every value it asks for is published and locked and every checklist task of it is done. Ziffr looks again after each Lock, each time a checklist task is ticked off or closed, and in each daily run, and then does what the Workflow's Send Snapshot step says, once. Looking never undoes or stops the Lock or the tick-off that set it off, and a task reopened afterwards makes the period unfinished again but sends nothing twice. The Workflow page and periodstatus say whether a period is finished (finished, with the count of checklist tasks next to the…

sections.heading: Dashboards and Findings
sections.text:
A Dashboard is where you watch your Metrics as their values come in. This chapter goes through every screen and option that belongs to dashboards: the list of dashboards, building one, the menus of each Widget, Findings, presenting, sharing, View Links, Snapshots and Versions.
Everyone in a Workspace can open the dashboards they own and those shared with them. Members, Admins and Owners can also create dashboards. A Guest only looks at the dashboards shared with them and creates none. A Guest is never shown who else is in the Workspace: in a dashboard or a Snapshot, owners, Submitters and…

sections.heading: The Dashboards list
sections.text:
Choose Dashboards in the sidebar to see every dashboard you may open, in two groups:
Mine: the dashboards you made. Each says "Yours".
Shared with me: dashboards a colleague shared with you. Each says who it is from and whether you "can edit it" or "can look at it".
Your Home dashboard carries a small Home mark. Each card has a Pin button at its right: it pins the dashboard to the sidebar (see Pinning a dashboard).
At the top, if you may create dashboards:
If there is no dashboard yet, the list says "No dashboards yet" and suggests naming one or asking a colleague to share theirs. A Guest…

sections.heading: Your Home dashboard
sections.text:
Ziffr opens on your Home dashboard. You choose it yourself: open the dashboard, open its ⋯ menu and choose Home dashboard. The entry then shows a tick until you choose another. If you never chose one, Ziffr opens on the first dashboard you made, or else the first one shared with you. If your Home is no longer shared with you, the same rule picks another. A new Workspace, a trial included, opens on the Setup Guide first.
While you have no dashboard (or only a trial's untouched example that you did not choose as Home) and see no other Metric, Home asks Where would you like to start? instead.
A…

sections.heading: A new Workspace
sections.text: A new Workspace opens on the Setup Guide, not on an empty dashboard list; see Getting started. Until you make or are shown a dashboard, the list says "No dashboards yet", and Home offers where to start.

sections.heading: Opening a dashboard
sections.text:
A dashboard shows its name as a large heading. Below it, a line says whose it is: "Yours", or "Anna shared this with you as Editor" (or "as Viewer"). If the dashboard has an introduction, it follows.
Every Widget writes its values in the Workspace's Number Style with each Metric's unit, such as "118.941 €" or "$1,200". Chart axes step by round numbers (1, 2, 2.5 or 5 times a power of ten) and write all their labels one way, all shortened or all in full; a chart of a single value starts at 0. Axes and labels shorten values from 10,000 on, such as "12.3k", "126k €" or "1.2M", and changes read…

sections.heading: Pinning a dashboard
sections.text:
For the dashboards you open every day, press Pin in the row of buttons above a dashboard, or the pin on its card in the list. The button then reads Pinned; press it again to unpin. Pinned dashboards appear in the sidebar under Dashboards, in the order you pinned them. You can pin up to eight; with eight pinned, Ziffr says so and asks you to unpin one first.
Order: drag a pinned dashboard up or down in the sidebar. Without a mouse, open the ⋯ menu on its row and choose Move up or Move down; Unpin is there too.
A shrunk sidebar shows each pin as a small tile with its first letter; hover or…

sections.heading: Switching dashboards
sections.text:
The dashboard's name is also a button, and a long name wraps onto more lines rather than being cut off. Press it to open the switcher:
Find a dashboard: type part of a name to narrow the list.
Mine and Shared with me: the same two groups as on the list. The Home dashboard has a house mark; shared ones show their owner's name.
New dashboard (if you may create): opens the New dashboard window.
All dashboards: goes to the Dashboards list.

sections.heading: A dashboard you may not open
sections.text: If you follow a link to a dashboard that is not shared with you, Ziffr says "This dashboard isn't shared with you" and offers Ask Anna for access (with the owner's name). Ziffr tells the owner, who can grant you Viewer access or decline under Who can see this. You hear back either way. The dashboard's name stays hidden until then.

sections.heading: The toolbar
sections.text:
The buttons to the right of the name are:
Home dashboard and Pinned are in the ⋯ menu, each with a tick while it is on. Home dashboard makes this your Home dashboard (it cannot be switched off here: choose another dashboard as your Home instead). Pinned puts the dashboard in the sidebar or takes it out. In the demo, Pinned shows as off and says "Pinning is off in the demo". The switcher's list shows both marks too.
The ⋯ menu holds:
A deck's ⋯ menu has the same Who can see this and View links… entries, with the same panels (see Decks).
Theme… opens a small window with one list. Its first…

sections.heading: Gallery
sections.text: Gallery (the button beside New dashboard on the Dashboards page) shows the ways to draw a Metric, so you can see what is possible before you build anything. It lists every built-in view in groups (Views, Analyses, Findings), each drawn with one of your own Metrics: pick it under Show them with, or choose Sample data to see made-up numbers. Views that compare Metrics (a correlation, a matrix, Drivers, a Scoreboard) use your other Metrics that share the most months with the one you picked. A view your Metric cannot fill, such as a Finding that needs a breakdown it does not have, is drawn with…

sections.heading: Creating a dashboard
sections.text:
New dashboard in the switcher, From a template… on the list, and Create dashboard on an empty start screen all open the New dashboard window.
1. Name: required, up to 120 characters.
2. Start from: pick one choice. Empty dashboard means you add Widgets from the Pool yourself. Each Dashboard Template shows a Preview drawn with Sample Data, its description and how many Widgets it has; "from Ziffr" marks the built-in ones. (A Pack's Preview, before you install it, draws the Pack's Dashboard Templates under the Pack's own Metric names.) Ziffr ships eight (Overview, One metric in depth, Two…

sections.heading: Viewing and editing
sections.text:
A dashboard opens for looking. Its owner and Editors switch into editing on purpose with Edit; the button then reads Done. An empty dashboard that you may change opens in edit mode right away, since there is nothing to look at yet.
If you may only look, an empty dashboard says "This dashboard is empty." If you may change it, it says "Press Edit to add widgets."
A value that waits for Approval shows, marked "not approved yet" next to it, or "unapproved" in a table row; a locked period shows a lock. The Metric's own page marks such a value the same way.
A Widget with no values to draw says so…

sections.heading: What edit mode adds
sections.text:
The Pool appears on the left side (below the dashboard on a narrow screen).
Name and Introduction fields appear under the heading. The introduction says what the dashboard tells, in a sentence or two, up to 4,000 characters. It is shown above the dashboard and first in its Read view. Once you change either field, a Save name and introduction button appears.
Widgets can be moved and resized. Drag a Widget by its title bar (a grip appears when you point at it). Drag its lower right corner to resize it. A Widget is at least 2 columns wide and 3 rows high, out of 12 columns. The new layout is…

sections.heading: The Pool
sections.text:
Metrics that share a name show their owner (or, for one owner, the period and unit) next to the name in the Pool, so you can tell them apart.
A widget that shows an Archived Metric keeps drawing its history and is marked Archived next to its title; the Pool, a template's Slots and a panel's list of Metrics no longer offer it (a panel keeps one it already shows, so you can take it out).
The Pool holds everything you can put on the dashboard. Filter at the top narrows all of it by name. It has three parts:
Metrics: every Metric you can see, except Archived Metrics. A derived Metric has a Σ…

sections.heading: Filling a Widget Template's Slots
